newsitem.title: USA: World output, use to blame for lower cotton prices.
newsitem.headline: World output, use to blame for lower cotton prices.

text.p: Robust global supplies, slack demand and quality problems have had a greater impact than imports on weaker cotton prices over the past year, a leading cotton industry official said.
"We don't see any evidence that raw cotton imports have had an appreciable effect on new crop prices," Gaylon Booker, vice president with the National Cotton Council (NCC), said.
"World supply and demand, more than anything else, has driven both the world price and the December New York contract."

The December 1997 contract, which farmers monitor closely to make decisions about planted acreage, has been trading around 77.00 cents per lb compared to 80.00 cents per lb last year, on the New York Cotton Exchange (NYCE).
As of 1235 EST Tuesday, December traded down 0.20 cent, to 76.40 cents.

The presentation to industry members at the annual Beltwide Cotton Conferences was prompted by concern over surging imports, and an NCC review of the the three-step program. The program was implemented as a way to keep U.S. cotton competitive on the global market when domestic prices were out of sync with world prices.
Step 3 allows foreign cotton to enter U.S. mills each week when when prices are 1.25 cents per lb higher than the A-index, the average of the five cheapest world growths, for ten consecutive weeks.

High U.S. cotton prices in relation to world prices have triggered imports each week since November 1995. Booker estimates the U.S. could import a record 800,000 480-lb bales during the 1995/96 and 1996/97 seasons, under the provision.
While conceding the number of foreign bales is high, he cautioned against program adjustments that would ease a transition from Step 3 to Step 2.

The second step allows U.S. textile mills and merchants to receive government subsidies when U.S. prices are more than 1.25 cents a lb above the A-index, for four consecutive weeks, and connot be triggered when the third step is in effect.

"The result would be more aggressive U.S. pricing in the world market," Booker said. "This would cause a downward pressure on the A-index and under most market conditions, a downward pressure on the NYCE contract."
Additionally, Step 2 would neither encourage textile mills to use domestic cotton nor stem imports, since mills are not purchasing foreign cotton at current price relationships.
Recent imports are the result of past purchases.

"Results of program changes to facilitate a transition from Step 3 to Step 2 would be mixed," Booker said. "The greatest returns would be long term and producers would need to be prepared for the possibility of some short term downward pressure on prices."
